issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: For a 35-year-old single male special education teacher reporting a mugging/robbery, 'I have failed in my most important role in life' is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The other appraisals center on self-blame and persistent danger, but this item implies a salient role failure theme (e.g. partner/parent/protector) that is not otherwise represented in triggers, threat, or memory.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: Within Memory, intense shame and intense rage on recall can coexist, but paired with a mugging/robbery and the rest of this profile they pull toward different meanings of the event without enough support elsewhere. Shame would usually connect to strong self-blame/humiliation themes, while rage would connect to injustice/anger themes; the profile does not integrate both clearly.

vignette: Daniel, a 35-year-old special education teacher, had always felt a strong sense of security in his life, which made the events of one fateful evening all the more jarring. Walking home from a late meeting at school, he was suddenly approached by two men who demanded his wallet. As they shouted at him, the fear gripped his chest, rendering him paralyzed. The memory of that night replayed in his mind with excruciating clarity, almost like a series of photographs he could not escape. The shouts of his assailants echoed in his head, a trigger that sent him spiraling into a panicked state whenever he encountered similar sounds, like yelling in the classroom or on the street. Each time he heard those familiar shouts, it was as if the memory of that night flooded his mind uncontrollably, allowing the fear and panic he had felt to re-emerge in vivid detail. The moment those sounds pierced the air, Daniel found himself back in that dark street, every detail of the traumatic event rushing back, as if he were reliving it all over again. Each time he heard those familiar shouts, they pulled the memory of the mugging into sharp focus, making him feel as though he were once again trapped in that moment of fear. This recollection not only brought back the intense fear he had felt but also a deep-seated rage at himself-why hadn't he been more cautious? Once the memory had surfaced, it was as if the danger of that night was still present, making every situation feel fraught with potential harm. Why had he let his guard down? This guilt compounded with each flashback, transforming his memories into a tormenting cycle of self-recrimination. Each time the guilt resurfaced, it intensified the sense of threat he felt, as if he were constantly under scrutiny for not having acted differently. These negative thoughts solidified his feeling that he was unworthy of safety, making every situation feel like a potential threat, reinforcing his belief that he was always in danger. Since the incident, Daniel found it increasingly difficult to relax, even in the safety of his own home. He could not shake the feeling that danger lurked just beyond his front door. When he entered any room, whether it was the staff lounge at school or a café on his way home, he instinctively scanned for exits, a habit that had developed into an almost compulsive behavior. The need to be on guard consumed him, and with it came a profound sense of inadequacy. He often caught himself thinking that someone else would have handled the situation better and that he had somehow failed. This constant sense of danger reinforced his negative appraisals, leading him to believe that he was fundamentally incapable of managing his own safety. This incessant self-criticism was a direct response to the unrelenting threat he felt, leading him to conclude that he was incapable of managing his own safety, eroding his self-worth further. His negative appraisals reinforced a growing belief that danger was ever-present, making him feel perpetually vulnerable and unworthy of protection. The constant hypervigilance left him drained, yet he felt he had no choice; being alert was the only way to protect himself from another potential threat. This pervasive sense of threat seemed to confirm his belief that he was unworthy of safety, reinforcing the idea that he was always in danger and could not trust his own judgment. The memories of the mugging were not just painful; they were overwhelming, stirring up a cocktail of emotions that left him feeling trapped. Each time Daniel recalled the event, he was flooded with rage and guilt, a visceral reminder of how vulnerable he had become. This emotional turmoil further fueled his sense of threat. He was convinced that the world was a dangerous place, and he was inadequate for not being able to fend off such a threat when it mattered most. The more he believed he was incapable of protecting himself, the more intense his memories felt, as if they were reminders of just how vulnerable he truly was. Each recollection pushed him deeper into a cycle of fear and self-blame, with the memory of the mugging illuminating his perceived failures as a person. "Each time the anxiety surged, the memory of the mugging followed closely behind, as if the fear he felt in those moments drew the recollections to the forefront of his mind with an unrelenting grip." The heightened sense of threat that accompanied those recollections kept the memories fresh and vivid in his mind, as if danger was a constant presence he had to keep revisiting to understand. His persistent feeling of being in danger made the memories surge to the forefront of his mind, demanding attention and reinforcing the narrative that he was not safe anywhere. With each encounter that heightened his sense of danger, he felt the memories rise to the surface, almost demanding his attention, as if the past was a lesson he had yet to fully grasp. He often reflected that he should have been able to prevent it, leading him to scrutinize his actions and choices relentlessly. The presence of authority figures became another source of anxiety for Daniel. Whenever he encountered police officers, he was overwhelmed by a sense of panic. He felt as though he was being judged, with their mere presence triggering the painful memories of his experience. This sense of being judged further amplified his perception of threat, leading him to believe that he was under constant scrutiny, which made the memories of the mugging feel even more relevant and imminent. This continual association of authority with danger further exacerbated his feelings of inadequacy and threat. He could not escape the notion that the world was out to get him, and the cascading effect of these thoughts made it increasingly difficult for him to function. Daniel's teaching suffered as he withdrew from social interactions at work, becoming less engaged with his students and colleagues. The ongoing threat he felt made him believe he was unworthy of connection, further entrenching his feelings of inadequacy and isolation. His once-vibrant classroom felt stifled by his anxiety, as he struggled to balance his role as an educator with the turmoil raging inside him. The pressure of feeling unsafe at work made the memories flood back at unexpected moments, robbing him of focus and clarity, as he constantly scanned the room for potential threats. With each new trigger, the threat he felt only deepened his negative appraisals, convincing him that he was failing to keep himself safe and highlighting his inadequacies. "This pervasive feeling of inadequacy transformed into a belief that he was a target for harm, making each new encounter feel laden with potential threats, as though he was walking into a minefield with every step he took." After months of grappling with these feelings, Daniel finally sought help. "The more he felt threatened, the more the memories surged forth, demanding his attention as if to remind him of the danger he believed he was perpetually in." The weight of his experiences had become too heavy to carry alone, and he hoped to reclaim the sense of safety and security he once felt. Deep down, he feared that he might never be able to escape the shadow of his past. What frightened him most was the thought that he would remain trapped in this cycle of anxiety and self-doubt forever. Yet, as he sat in the therapist's office, he also held onto a glimmer of hope-that through addressing his trauma, he might find a way to heal and reclaim the life he once knew.

The memory of that night replayed in his mind with excruciating clarity, almost like a series of photographs he could not escape. The shouts of his assailants echoed in his head, a trigger that sent him spiraling into a panicked state whenever he encountered similar sounds, like yelling in the classroom or on the street. Each time he heard those familiar shouts, it was as if the memory of that night flooded his mind uncontrollably, allowing the fear and panic he had felt to re-emerge in vivid detail. The moment those sounds pierced the air, Daniel found himself back in that dark street, every detail of the traumatic event rushing back, as if he were reliving it all over again. Each time he heard those familiar shouts, they pulled the memory of the mugging into sharp focus, making him feel as though he were once again trapped in that moment of fear. This recollection not only brought back the intense fear he had felt but also a deep-seated rage at himself—why hadn’t he been more cautious? Once the memory had surfaced, it was as if the danger of that night was still present, making every situation feel fraught with potential harm. Why had he let his guard down? This guilt compounded with each flashback, transforming his memories into a tormenting cycle of self-recrimination. Each time the guilt resurfaced, it intensified the sense of threat he felt, as if he were constantly under scrutiny for not having acted differently.
